title: Sewing a button onto knitting
subtitle: Attaching a button securely through knitted fabric so it stays put through washing and use.
excerpt: Attaching a button to a knitted garment requires a slightly different approach from sewing buttons onto woven fabric. The stretchy, open structure of knitting means the thread must be anchored through multiple layers and a thread shank built up underneath the button so the fabric can move freely.
sourceNotes: Standard UK needlework and finishing technique. Weldon's Practical Knitter finishing notes describe button attachment on knitted garments. General UK sewing and needlework tradition.
heroPrompt: A sewing needle threading matching yarn through the holes of a wooden button attached to a ribbed knitted band, the stitches neat and even.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small column of thread or yarn built up between the back of the button and the surface of the fabric, which allows the button to sit away from the fabric and lets the buttonhole layer close over it easily.

content.text: Knitting is elastic and open-structured, so buttons sewn through a single layer of fabric can pull the stitches out of shape over time. To attach a button securely, the thread is anchored through two or three passes of the fabric, a backing button is placed behind the main fabric where the knitting is particularly loose, and a
is built up to lift the button slightly away from the surface. Difficulty: beginner.
A sewing needle with an eye large enough for the thread or fine yarn
Thread or fine yarn in a matching colour (for large buttons on a knitted button band, a strand of the project yarn split to a finer weight works well)
A small flat backing button (optional but recommended for loose knitted fabrics)
A cocktail stick or second needle to hold the shank gap while wrapping (optional)
Mark the button position on the band. Overlap the two fronts and push a pin through the buttonhole to the band beneath.
Thread the needle with a doubled length of thread or yarn. Knot the end and bring the needle up from the wrong side of the band at the marked point.
If using a backing button, thread it onto the needle from the wrong side first. Slide it down to the fabric to sit against the wrong side.
Place the button on the right side. Lay a cocktail stick or a spare needle across the top of the button and sew through the button holes over this stick. This builds in the shank gap as you sew.
Sew through the button holes 4-6 times, passing the needle through both layers of the band each time.

Remove the stick. Pull the button away from the fabric to expose the threads beneath. Wrap the thread around these threads several times to form the shank, then pass the needle to the wrong side, knot off, and trim.

Buttons appear on cardigans, knitted jackets, bag closures, and cushion backs. Any pattern with a button band will need this technique at the finishing stage. The same method applies to press-stud and hook-and-eye placement on knitted garments.

items.symptom: The button pulls the knitted band out of shape
items.cause: Thread was sewn through too few stitches, or no backing button was used
items.fix: Always anchor through at least two or three stitches of the knitted fabric on each pass. Use a flat backing button on the wrong side to spread the load across more fabric.

items.symptom: The button sits flat against the fabric and the buttonhole layer will not close over it
items.cause: No thread shank was built up
items.fix: Remove the button and re-sew using the cocktail-stick method to create a shank of at least 3-4 mm for a standard button.

items.symptom: The thread breaks after a few uses
items.cause: Thread too thin for the weight of the button, or the garment
items.fix: Use a doubled thread or switch to a single strand of the project yarn. For heavy buttons on chunky knits, use a strong thread such as button thread or carpet thread.
